c.tagline: High-altitude gateway to the Tibetan world, immortalized in the Kangding Love Song

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis are cheap and plentiful in town; drivers rarely speak English, so having your destination written in Chinese characters helps.

emergency.note: Police 110, ambulance 120, fire 119. This is a remote high-altitude area — English-speaking help is scarce, and altitude sickness is a real risk on arrival; acclimatize before strenuous activity.

avoid.reason: No notable crime areas, but watch for stray dogs on hillside trails and take a day to acclimatize to the 2,560 m altitude.

hood_desc: The historic core along the Zheduo and Yala rivers, packed with noodle shops, Tibetan handicraft stalls, and the golden-roofed Anjue Temple. This is where the Kangding Love Song was said to be born, and it's the most walkable, atmospheric part of town.

The narrow ribbon of town squeezed along the fast-flowing Zheduo River, lined with guesthouses and hotpot restaurants. Evenings bring locals out for riverside strolls and impromptu Tibetan dancing in the small plazas.

Kangding's newer, more modern district near the long-distance bus station, with supermarkets, chain hotels, and easier road access toward Chengdu and Litang. Less charming but convenient for logistics.
lodging: Kangding Love Song Plaza Yoyo City Gesang Flower Hotel

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as locals do.

transit.pay: Cash or mobile pay (WeChat/Alipay) on board
transit.map: No official transit app; town is small enough to navigate on foot
transit.note: Kangding proper is compact and best explored on foot; buses and shared vans link the bus station, old town, and Mugecuo trailhead.

bus: Long-distance buses to/from Chengdu (5-6 hrs) via the Sichuan-Tibet Highway

car.idp: Not valid — foreign licenses/IDPs are not accepted for driving in China

tip.r: Tipping is not customary anywhere in China, including Kangding; it can even confuse service staff.

food.name: Yak Earthenware Hotpot
food.desc: Chunks of yak simmered for hours in a clay pit-pot with radish, potato and highland herbs, then ladled out at the table; the plateau's shared meal.

places.name: A Xi Tu Tao Yak Pot
places.note: Built around the Tibetan pit-pot yak soup; also matsutake chicken soup.

places.name: Lamaya Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Tibetan-decorated dining room known for its yak and beef dishes.

places.name: Zheduo riverside restaurants
places.note: Cluster of larger Sichuan-Tibetan places doing hotpot along the river.

food.name: Tibetan Momo
food.desc: Steamed or pan-fried dumplings pleated around minced yak and onion, eaten with chilli sauce; sold from breakfast onwards across the old town.

places.name: Lamaya Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Full Tibetan menu; momo alongside butter tea and tsampa.

places.name: Kangding old town market stalls
places.note: Morning steamer baskets of yak momo at street prices.

places.name: A Xi Tu Tao Yak Pot
places.note: Yak dumplings as a side to the pit-pot; generous plateau portions.

food.name: Tsampa
food.desc: Roasted highland barley flour kneaded by hand with butter tea into a dough ball; the staple Tibetan energy food, still eaten daily here.

places.name: Lamaya Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Roasted barley flour served the traditional way with buttered tea.

places.name: Kangding old town market stalls
places.note: Barley flour and butter sold loose beside the pilgrim shops.

places.name: Tangsubao
places.note: Yak-product shop and eatery stocking tsampa, butter and dried meat.

food.name: Air-Dried Yak Meat
food.desc: Strips of yak hung to dry in cold mountain air, then eaten cured or lightly fried with chilli; salty, chewy and intensely beefy.

places.name: Tangsubao
places.note: Marketplace for all things yak, including dried meat to take away.

places.name: Lamaya Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Serves dried yak as a starter with barley staples.

places.name: Kangding old town market stalls
places.note: Vendors sell it by weight; ask for the softer fried version.

food.name: Beef Noodle Soup
food.desc: The Kangding breakfast bowl: hand-cut wheat noodles in clear beef or yak broth, dosed with Sichuan pepper and pickled greens.

places.name: Zheduo riverside noodle shops
places.note: Family-run counters along the rushing river, open from early morning.

places.name: Kangding old town market stalls
places.note: Cheapest bowls in town, eaten standing before the temple opens.

places.name: Lamaya Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down version with Tibetan thukpa-style noodles.

food.name: Matsutake Chicken Soup
food.desc: Highland matsutake mushrooms simmered with free-range chicken into a clear, perfumed broth; a summer and autumn speciality of the Garze mountains.

places.name: A Xi Tu Tao Yak Pot

places.name: Kangding old town market stalls
places.note: Fresh matsutake sold by foragers in late summer.

food.name: Yak Butter Tea (Suyoucha)
food.desc: Brick tea churned with yak butter and salt into a warm, savoury drink; the standard hydration and calorie source above 2,500 metres.

food.desc: Cloudy, lightly fermented highland barley brew, low in alcohol and faintly sour; poured at Tibetan meals and festivals across Garze.

landmarks: Mugecuo Lake (Muge Tso)
A pristine alpine lake at 3,700 meters ringed by snow peaks, azalea forests and hot springs, the jewel of Kangding's high country.
Paoma Mountain (Paomashan)
The hill immortalized by the beloved 'Kangding Love Song' offers cable-car access to prayer-flag-draped temples and views over the valley town.
Nanwu Monastery
Kangding's most important Gelugpa monastery, where morning chants, butter lamps and debating monks offer an intimate taste of Tibetan Buddhism.
Anjue Temple (Ngachu Monastery)
A serene 17th-century Tibetan Buddhist temple in the town center, founded under the Fifth Dalai Lama's patronage, aglow with prayer wheels.
Zheduo Mountain Pass
The dramatic 4,298-meter gateway between Han China and the Tibetan plateau, its switchbacks and prayer flags delivering staggering snow-mountain panoramas.
Xinduqiao
Nicknamed the photographer's paradise, this high-plateau valley of golden poplars, Tibetan farmhouses and grazing yaks lies just over the Zheduo Pass.
Tagong Grassland and Tagong Monastery
Sweeping high-altitude grasslands where nomads race horses beneath sacred Mount Yala, beside a monastery treasured for its Sakyamuni statue.
Erdaoqiao Hot Springs
Centuries-old riverside hot springs just outside town, where travelers have soaked away Tea Horse Road fatigue since the Qing dynasty.
Kangding Old Town and Zheduo River Squares
Evenings bring locals dancing Tibetan guozhuang circles in riverside squares as the rushing Zheduo River thunders through the lantern-lit gorge town.
Jingang Temple (Vajra Monastery)
A tranquil Nyingma-school monastery on Kangding's southern edge, its golden roofs and giant prayer wheels framed by steep green mountainsides.

train.note: Kangding has no railway station of any kind, so there are neither international nor domestic trains; the Sichuan-Tibet railway that will eventually serve the area is still under construction. The nearest useful railheads are in Chengdu, from where the journey is completed by road over the Erlang Shan pass. Until the line opens, buses and the small Kangding Airport are the only scheduled ways in.

bus.note: There are no international coaches; Kangding sits deep inside Sichuan, far from any border. Long-distance buses from Chengdu (Xinnanmen and Chadianzi terminals) run roughly 07:00-13:00 and take 8-11 hours for about ¥141, and the Kangding bus terminal at the northern end of town is a ten-minute walk from the centre. Onward Tibetan-plateau services run from the same terminal to Tagong (about 4 hours, ¥40) and Litang (about 9 hours, ¥81); seats are bought at the counter and sell out early in summer.

ferry.note: Kangding is a mountain town on the eastern edge of the Tibetan plateau, hundreds of kilometres from the sea and on rivers far too steep to navigate, so there are no passenger ferry services of any kind.

full.name: Hailuogou Glacier
full.blurb: A glacier descends from Gongga Mountain, Sichuan's highest peak, through forest down to around 2,850 meters, with hot springs near its base.

full.name: Danba
full.blurb: Stone watchtowers up to 60 meters tall rise above Tibetan villages scattered across steep valleys in a district known as the 'Thousand Watchtower County'.

full.name: Litang
full.blurb: A high-altitude Tibetan grassland town over 4,000 meters up holds a 16th-century monastery founded with support from the Third Dalai Lama.
